subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Primary data' is best defined as data that is:
options: Collected first-hand by the researcher for their own study
questions.explain: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher, e.g. via questionnaires, interviews or observation.

questions.q: 'Representativeness' of a sample refers to whether:
options: The sample accurately reflects the wider population so findings can be generalised
The sample is large enough to be cheap
questions.explain: Representativeness concerns whether a sample mirrors the target population so that findings can be generalised.

questions.q: 'Covert participant observation' means the researcher:
options: Joins the group and openly tells members they are being studied
Watches from a distance using a survey
Joins the group secretly, without revealing they are a researcher
questions.explain: In covert participant observation the researcher's identity and purpose are hidden from the group being studied.

questions.q: In sociological research, 'PET' factors stand for:
questions.explain: PET factors influencing choice of method are the practical, ethical and theoretical considerations.

questions.q: Interpretivists tend to prefer:
options: Qualitative methods that explore meanings and understanding
questions.explain: Interpretivists favour qualitative methods to understand the meanings and motives behind people's actions.

questions.q: A 'representative' sample is one that:
options: Reflects the wider population so findings can be generalised
Contains only volunteers who feel strongly
questions.explain: A representative sample mirrors the target population, allowing findings to be generalised to it.

questions.q: A strength of participant observation favoured by interpretivists is that it:
options: Produces large amounts of quantitative data
Is highly reliable and easily repeated
Gives a valid, in-depth insight into people's real behaviour and meanings
questions.explain: Participant observation is valued by interpretivists for the valid, in-depth understanding it gives of people's real-world behaviour.

questions.q: Which is a key ethical issue researchers must consider?
options: Making the study as expensive as possible
Gaining informed consent and protecting participants from harm
questions.explain: Ethical research requires informed consent, confidentiality and protecting participants from harm.

questions.q: 'Validity' in research refers to whether:
options: The results can be repeated to get the same findings
The data gives a true, authentic picture of what it claims to measure
questions.explain: Validity is about whether data is genuine and accurately reflects reality, giving a true picture.

questions.q: A 'pilot study' is:
options: The final stage of a project
A small-scale trial run carried out before the main research
questions.explain: A pilot study is a small trial run used to test and refine the research method before the main study.

questions.q: A key ethical problem with covert observation is that:
options: It is impossible to carry out
Participants cannot give informed consent because they do not know they are studied
questions.explain: Covert observation raises ethical concerns because participants are deceived and cannot give informed consent.

questions.q: A 'sampling frame' is:
options: A list of all the members of the population from which a sample is drawn
A picture frame in the research room
questions.explain: A sampling frame is the list of all members of the research population from which the sample is selected.

questions.q: 'Secondary data' refers to data that:
options: Is always more reliable than primary data
Is collected first-hand by the researcher
Already exists, having been produced by others (e.g. official statistics, documents)
questions.explain: Secondary data already exists and was produced by others, such as official statistics or existing documents.

questions.q: A practical advantage of using official statistics is that they are usually:
options: Already available, cheap and cover large numbers of people
questions.explain: Official statistics are a cheap, readily available secondary source covering large populations, though they may lack validity.

questions.q: A 'structured interview' is one in which:
options: The interviewer asks the same set of pre-decided questions in a fixed order
No questions are asked at all
The conversation is free-flowing with no set questions
questions.explain: A structured interview uses a fixed set of standardised questions, making it more reliable but often less in-depth.

questions.q: Positivists tend to favour methods that produce:
options: Quantitative data and seek to find patterns and causes scientifically
questions.explain: Positivists prefer quantitative, scientific methods to identify patterns and causal laws in social behaviour.

questions.q: Quantitative data is data in the form of:
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical, allowing measurement and statistical comparison.

questions.q: A strength of postal/self-completion questionnaires is that they:
options: Can reach large numbers of people quickly and cheaply
Always achieve a very high response rate
questions.explain: Questionnaires can gather data from many people quickly and cheaply, though response rates and depth can be limited.

questions.q: An 'unstructured interview' is one that:
options: Is more like a guided conversation, allowing flexible, open-ended responses
Uses a fixed list of identical questions for everyone
Can only be done by post
questions.explain: An unstructured interview is informal and flexible, like a conversation, producing detailed qualitative data.

questions.q: 'Non-participant observation' means the researcher:
options: Joins in fully with the group's activities
Observes the group without taking part in their activities
questions.explain: In non-participant observation the researcher watches the group without joining in their activities.

questions.q: 'Reliability' in research refers to whether:
options: A study can be repeated and produce consistent results
questions.explain: Reliability means a method can be repeated by others and produce consistent, similar results.

questions.q: Interpretivists criticise laboratory experiments in studying people because:
options: They are too cheap to run
The artificial setting may produce unnatural behaviour, lowering validity
questions.explain: Interpretivists argue the artificial lab setting can cause people to behave unnaturally, reducing the validity of results.
